# Malaysia-bound workers keep asking when they can leave. Recruiters have no answer yet

Medical tests, migration costs and departure dates remain unsettled as agencies urge govt to quickly complete recruitment procedures

Published : 21 September 2026

•

Updated : 21 September 2026, 17:33

• [WORK AND MIGRATION](/news/work-and-migration)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Star Online Report

![malay.jpg](/sites/default/files/styles/big_1/public/2026-09/malay.jpg?h=d1cb525d)

File photo

Prospective workers hoping to go to Malaysia are still waiting to know when medical tests will begin, how much migration will cost, and when they will be able to leave, despite moves to resume recruitment to one of Bangladesh's major labour markets.

Recruiting agency owners today urged the government to quickly finalise the remaining procedures, reopen the market and start sending workers, saying prospective workers were regularly turning up at their offices seeking answers.

[Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source ![google-preferred-source-badge](/themes/custom/swallow/images/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.webp)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=thedailystar.net)

“Workers come to our offices asking when medical tests will start, when they can go and how much it will cost. We cannot give them an answer,” said Atiqur Rahman Biswas, owner of recruiting agency Al Aqaba Associates, while responding to journalists at a press briefing at the National Press Club.

Image

![](/sites/default/files/styles/big_4/public/2026-09/malaysia.jpg?h=ffaa6ea2)

***Photo: Star***

A section of the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (Baira) members organised the briefing and highlighted the importance of the Malaysian market, saying the minimum basic wage there is 1,700 ringgit and a Bangladeshi worker can earn around Tk 60,000 to Tk 70,000 a month including overtime.

Malaysia stopped taking new foreign workers from Bangladesh and other source countries from June 1, 2024, after reaching its foreign-worker ceiling.

Malaysia again allowed recruitment from source countries in August 2025, after which countries including Nepal and Myanmar began sending workers, while Bangladesh could not take advantage of the opportunity at the time.

The latest recruitment arrangement has, however, triggered a dispute among recruiters over whether effective control would remain with 25 principal agencies.

A group of Baira members earlier alleged that allowing another 312 agencies to work as associates would make little difference if they could not send workers against their own job orders and licences without going through the principals. They demanded direct access to Malaysia's Foreign Workers Centralised Management System for all qualified agencies.

Atiqur Rahman and Abdul Gafur Bhuiyan, a former senior vice-president of Baira, rejected the syndication allegation.

They said the 312 associates could collect job demand, communicate with employers, and recruit workers, but processing would have to go through one of the 25 principal agencies or the state-run Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL).

Gafur said an associate agency could choose the principal agency it wished to work through, and urged the government to gradually include other eligible agencies in the process.

The expatriates' welfare ministry earlier said the arrangement covers 25 directly selected agencies, 312 associates and BOESL -- 338 entities in total. It also said the detailed recruitment procedure was still being finalised and advised prospective workers not to pay money, undergo medical tests or hand over passports until formal instructions were issued.

Atiqur also rejected claims that workers would have to spend Tk 6 lakh to Tk 8 lakh, saying the agencies themselves had not yet been informed about the final migration cost.

He said the current mechanism was being pursued under the existing Bangladesh-Malaysia memorandum of understanding, which remains effective until December 31 this year.

The expatriates' welfare ministry earlier gave the same validity period.

Explaining how the agencies were selected, Atiqur said Malaysia had set criteria for Bangladeshi recruiters and the interim government invited interested agencies to apply, seeking information including their office facilities and manpower.

He said 423 agencies applied, and after scrutiny, their names were sent to Malaysia.

The ministry also said Malaysia selected the 25 principal agencies from a list of 423 prepared by the interim government. Malaysia initially selected the 25 agencies before subsequent discussions led to the inclusion of the 312 associates, Atiqur said.

The organisers said around 4.76 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia between August 2022 and May 31, 2024.

Gafur also referred to the government's announcement that Malaysia had agreed in principle to recruit 10,000 Bangladeshi workers without migration costs, with the workers to be sent through BOESL. No departure date has yet been announced.

The organisers accused a section of recruiters of politicising the dispute and trying to obstruct the recruitment process, and warned that prolonged disagreements could again put the Malaysian labour market at risk.
